primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: C2 deficiency impairs formation of the classical and lectin pathway C3 convertase and predisposes to infection and lupus-like autoimmunity
mechanism: C2 is cleaved during classical and lectin pathway activation and combines with C4b to form the pathway's C3 convertase. Complete C2 deficiency therefore markedly reduces classical-pathway hemolytic activity while leaving the alternative pathway intact and is associated with recurrent bacterial infections and lupus-like autoimmune disease, in part because early classical complement participates in clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic material.
vignette: A 14-year-old girl has recurrent bacterial sinus infections and develops photosensitive facial rash and inflammatory arthritis. Testing shows undetectable total classical-pathway hemolytic activity (CH50) with preserved alternative-pathway activity (AH50). Serum C3 and C4 concentrations are normal, and an individual complement-component assay shows absent C2.
lead: Which complement function is most directly lost as a result of this deficiency?
correct: Formation of the C3 convertase used by the classical and lectin pathways
distractors: Assembly of the alternative-pathway C3 convertase from C3b and factor B
Regulation of spontaneous alternative-pathway activation by factor H
Formation of the terminal membrane attack complex from C5b through C9
Inhibition of activated C1 proteases by C1 esterase inhibitor
distractor_notes: The alternative-pathway C3 convertase uses C3b and factor B and does not require C2, consistent with the preserved AH50 in the stem.
Factor H restrains the alternative pathway by regulating C3b; this function is independent of C2.
C5b-C9 form the membrane attack complex downstream of C3 activation. C2 deficiency primarily blocks the upstream classical/lectin C3-convertase step rather than deleting terminal complement proteins.
C1 esterase inhibitor limits activated C1r/C1s and kallikrein-related proteases; its deficiency causes hereditary angioedema and is not the defect shown here.
key_expl: C2 is an early component shared by the classical and lectin pathways. After cleavage, its active fragment associates with C4b to generate the C3 convertase for these pathways. Thus C2 deficiency abolishes classical-pathway function while sparing the alternative pathway and can produce both recurrent infection and lupus-like autoimmunity.
objective: Explain the functional consequence of C2 deficiency by linking loss of an early classical/lectin complement component to failure of that pathway's C3-convertase formation, low CH50 with preserved AH50, and susceptibility to infection and lupus-like autoimmunity.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Carotid sinus stretch is conveyed to the nucleus tractus solitarius through glossopharyngeal afferent fibers
mechanism: Increased arterial pressure stretches carotid sinus baroreceptors and increases afferent firing through the sinus nerve of Hering, a branch of cranial nerve IX, to the nucleus tractus solitarius. Central integration then decreases sympathetic output and increases vagal efferent activity, lowering heart rate and vascular tone.
vignette: During a physiology study, brief external pressure is applied over the carotid sinus of a healthy volunteer. Heart rate and arterial pressure fall transiently. In a second trial, a local nerve block selectively abolishes sensory transmission from the carotid sinus while leaving vagal efferent function intact; the hemodynamic response disappears.
lead: The blocked afferent fibers travel primarily in which cranial nerve?
distractors: Facial nerve (cranial nerve VII)
Vagus nerve (cranial nerve X)
Accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI)
Hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII)
distractor_notes: The facial nerve carries branchial motor, taste, and parasympathetic functions but is not the principal carotid sinus baroreceptor afferent pathway.
The vagus nerve carries aortic arch baroreceptor afferents and cardiac parasympathetic efferents, but carotid sinus afferents travel mainly through cranial nerve IX.
The accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius motor function and does not carry carotid sinus baroreceptor afferents.
The hypoglossal nerve provides motor innervation to the tongue and does not mediate the carotid baroreflex.
key_expl: Carotid sinus mechanoreceptor afferents pass through the sinus nerve of Hering into the glossopharyngeal nerve and terminate in the nucleus tractus solitarius. Aortic arch baroreceptor afferents instead travel through the vagus nerve.
objective: Distinguish the glossopharyngeal afferent limb of the carotid sinus baroreflex from the vagal afferent limb of the aortic arch reflex and the vagal efferent response to the heart.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Hartnup disease from SLC6A19 dysfunction impairs apical sodium-dependent neutral amino-acid transport in intestine and proximal tubule
mechanism: SLC6A19 encodes B0AT1, a sodium-dependent, chloride-independent transporter for neutral amino acids at the apical surface of intestinal epithelium and proximal tubular cells. Defective transport causes neutral aminoaciduria and intestinal loss, including tryptophan depletion that can reduce niacin synthesis and produce pellagra-like photosensitive and neurologic manifestations.
vignette: A 10-year-old boy has intermittent photosensitive dermatitis and episodes of gait instability during periods of poor nutrition. Urine amino-acid analysis shows generalized neutral aminoaciduria without increased cystine or dibasic amino acids. Blood glucose is normal and there is no glucosuria.
lead: Which epithelial transport process is most likely defective?
correct: Sodium-dependent apical transport of neutral amino acids by B0AT1 (SLC6A19)
distractors: Apical transport of cystine and dibasic amino acids by the b0,+ amino-acid transporter
Sodium-glucose cotransport by SGLT2 in the proximal tubule
Proton-coupled uptake of dipeptides and tripeptides by PEPT1 in the small intestine
Basolateral export of neutral amino acids from enterocytes into portal blood
distractor_notes: Defective b0,+ transport causes cystinuria with urinary cystine and dibasic amino acids, which the stem explicitly excludes.
SGLT2 handles glucose rather than neutral amino acids; normal blood glucose without glucosuria argues against a proximal glucose-transport defect.
PEPT1 absorbs small peptides and remains an alternate route for dietary amino-acid acquisition; Hartnup disease specifically affects neutral free-amino-acid transport by B0AT1.
The defining SLC6A19 defect is at the apical surface of intestinal and proximal tubular epithelia, not the generic basolateral amino-acid exit step.
key_expl: Hartnup disease is caused by defective B0AT1/SLC6A19, a sodium-dependent neutral amino-acid transporter expressed at the apical membrane of intestine and proximal tubule. Loss of tryptophan can reduce endogenous niacin production, explaining pellagra-like photosensitive and neurologic symptoms.
objective: Recognize Hartnup disease and localize the defect to SLC6A19-mediated apical neutral amino-acid transport, distinguishing it from cystinuria, glucosuria, and peptide transport.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type II (Gordon syndrome) causes familial hyperkalemic hypertension through WNK-KLHL3-CUL3 dysregulation with increased distal convoluted tubule NCC activity
mechanism: PHAII is caused by pathogenic variants affecting WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, or CUL3 signaling. The phenotype reflects increased activity of the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal nephron, promoting sodium retention and hypertension while reducing distal sodium delivery and potassium excretion; hyperkalemic hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and suppressed renin are characteristic.
vignette: A 19-year-old man is evaluated for hypertension. Blood pressure is 154/96 mm Hg. Serum potassium is 5.9 mEq/L, chloride is 113 mEq/L, bicarbonate is 18 mEq/L, and creatinine is normal. Plasma renin activity is suppressed. His father and older sister developed the same electrolyte pattern as teenagers. Neither patient uses medications or potassium supplements.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this patient's findings?
distractors: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess
Liddle syndrome
Pseudohypoaldosteronism type I
Hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism from diabetic kidney disease
distractor_notes: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess causes hypertension with suppressed renin but typically produces hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis from unopposed mineralocorticoid-receptor activation.
Liddle syndrome causes early hypertension with low renin and aldosterone but usually produces hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis due to increased ENaC activity.
Pseudohypoaldosteronism type I causes renal salt wasting, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis, typically with volume depletion and elevated renin/aldosterone rather than familial hypertension.

Hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism can cause hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis but usually occurs with diabetes or chronic kidney disease; the normal renal function, teenage familial hypertension, and autosomal dominant pattern favor PHAII.
key_expl: The combination of familial early hypertension, hyperkalemia despite normal GFR, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, and suppressed renin is characteristic of pseudohypoaldosteronism type II (familial hyperkalemic hypertension/Gordon syndrome). WNK-KLHL3-CUL3 pathway dysregulation increases thiazide-sensitive NCC activity, and the abnormalities respond strongly to thiazide therapy.
objective: Diagnose pseudohypoaldosteronism type II from familial hyperkalemic hypertension with normal GFR, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, and suppressed renin, and distinguish it from other inherited mineralocorticoid-like syndromes.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Acetazolamide inhibits proximal tubular carbonic anhydrase and causes bicarbonaturia with metabolic acidosis
mechanism: Carbonic anhydrase facilitates proximal tubular bicarbonate reclamation by enabling conversion between carbon dioxide, water, carbonic acid, bicarbonate, and hydrogen ions. Acetazolamide inhibits this process, reducing sodium bicarbonate reabsorption and increasing urinary bicarbonate loss, which lowers serum bicarbonate.
vignette: A 31-year-old climber begins acetazolamide before a rapid ascent to high altitude. After several doses, serum bicarbonate is lower than baseline and urinary bicarbonate excretion is increased.
lead: Which nephron effect most directly accounts for this acid-base change?
correct: Reduced proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption due to carbonic anhydrase inhibition
distractors: Reduced sodium-potassium-2 chloride cotransport in the thick ascending limb
Reduced sodium-chloride cotransport in the distal convoluted tubule
Reduced epithelial sodium channel activity in principal cells
Reduced mineralocorticoid receptor activation in collecting-duct principal cells
distractor_notes: Inhibition of NKCC2 is the mechanism of loop diuretics and does not directly explain acetazolamide-induced bicarbonaturia.
Inhibition of the distal convoluted tubule sodium-chloride cotransporter is the mechanism of thiazide diuretics, not carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
ENaC inhibition is produced by potassium-sparing agents such as amiloride and is not the primary proximal tubular action of acetazolamide.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism occurs with spironolactone or eplerenone and does not cause the characteristic proximal bicarbonate loss of acetazolamide.
key_expl: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, decreasing bicarbonate reclamation. The resulting bicarbonaturia lowers serum bicarbonate and produces a metabolic acidosis that helps stimulate ventilation at altitude.
objective: Connect acetazolamide therapy to proximal tubular carbonic anhydrase inhibition, bicarbonaturia, and reduced serum bicarbonate, and distinguish this mechanism from other diuretic targets.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Weber syndrome results from a ventral midbrain lesion affecting ipsilateral oculomotor fascicles and the cerebral peduncle
mechanism: A ventral midbrain lesion can injure exiting oculomotor nerve fascicles together with descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers in the cerebral peduncle. This produces an ipsilateral third-nerve palsy with contralateral weakness.
vignette: A 68-year-old man suddenly develops left-sided ptosis. The left eye rests down and out and the left pupil is dilated. Strength is markedly reduced in the right arm and leg, but sensation is intact and there is no prominent tremor or limb ataxia.
lead: Which pair of structures is most likely injured by the same lesion?
correct: Left oculomotor fascicles and left cerebral peduncle
distractors: Left oculomotor fascicles and left red nucleus
Left trochlear fascicles and left superior cerebellar peduncle
Left abducens fascicles and left corticospinal tract in the ventral pons
Left medial longitudinal fasciculus and left medial lemniscus
distractor_notes: Involvement of the red nucleus with oculomotor fascicles is associated with contralateral tremor or ataxia rather than the predominantly pyramidal weakness described.
Trochlear and superior cerebellar peduncle lesions do not produce the classic ipsilateral third-nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis.
A ventral pontine lesion involving the abducens fascicles and corticospinal tract would cause an ipsilateral sixth-nerve deficit rather than the third-nerve findings in the vignette.
A medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and medial lemniscus injury would affect contralateral vibration/proprioception rather than produce this pattern.
key_expl: Ipsilateral complete oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis localizes to the ventral midbrain. The lesion involves CN III fascicles and descending corticospinal/corticobulbar fibers in the cerebral peduncle, the classic anatomic substrate of Weber syndrome.
objective: Localize a ventral midbrain lesion by pairing ipsilateral oculomotor fascicle injury with contralateral pyramidal weakness from cerebral-peduncle involvement.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Pycnodysostosis from CTSK loss of function impairs osteoclast degradation of demineralized collagenous bone matrix
mechanism: CTSK encodes cathepsin K, a lysosomal cysteine protease highly expressed by osteoclasts. Osteoclasts in pycnodysostosis can acidify and demineralize bone, but cathepsin K deficiency markedly impairs degradation of type I collagen and other bone-matrix proteins, producing osteosclerosis with brittle bones and characteristic acroosteolysis and delayed cranial-suture closure.
vignette: An 11-year-old boy has short stature and several low-impact fractures. Radiographs show diffuse osteosclerosis, acroosteolysis of the distal phalanges, and persistently open cranial sutures. Serum electrolytes and acid-base studies are normal. Osteoclast numbers and ruffled borders are normal.
lead: Which osteoclast function is most specifically impaired in this disorder?
correct: Proteolytic degradation of demineralized type I collagen by cathepsin K
distractors: Generation of hydrogen ions for acidification of the resorption lacuna
Attachment to bone through integrin-dependent sealing-zone formation
Differentiation of osteoclast precursors in response to RANKL
Fusion of mononuclear precursors into multinucleated osteoclasts
distractor_notes: Defective proton generation or transport prevents mineral dissolution and causes other forms of osteopetrosis; pycnodysostosis specifically preserves demineralization but impairs degradation of the organic matrix.

The stem notes structurally normal osteoclasts with preserved ruffled borders; loss of sealing-zone formation would impair resorption globally rather than selectively eliminate cathepsin-K collagenolysis.
RANKL-RANK signaling governs osteoclast differentiation, but osteoclast numbers are normal in pycnodysostosis.
Failure of precursor fusion would reduce formation of multinucleated osteoclasts, inconsistent with the normal osteoclast number and morphology in the stem.
key_expl: Pycnodysostosis is caused by loss-of-function CTSK variants. Cathepsin K is the dominant osteoclastic lysosomal protease for type I collagen and other matrix proteins. Affected osteoclasts can demineralize bone but cannot efficiently digest the exposed organic matrix, producing dense yet fragile bone.
objective: Differentiate cathepsin-K deficiency from osteoclast acidification and differentiation defects by recognizing pycnodysostosis and identifying impaired proteolysis of demineralized type I collagen as the core defect.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency blocks conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA
mechanism: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is a mitochondrial enzyme that uses adenosylcobalamin, a vitamin B12-derived cofactor, to isomerize methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA during propionyl-CoA metabolism. Deficiency causes methylmalonic acid accumulation and episodes of high-anion-gap metabolic decompensation.
vignette: A 3-month-old infant develops vomiting, lethargy, tachypnea, and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis after protein feeding. Urine organic acid analysis shows markedly increased methylmalonic acid without homocystinuria. Cellular studies show normal uptake and formation of adenosylcobalamin.
lead: Which metabolic conversion is most directly impaired?
distractors: Homocysteine to methionine
Propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA
Pyruvate to acetyl-CoA
Branched-chain alpha-ketoacids to their acyl-CoA derivatives
distractor_notes: Homocysteine-to-methionine conversion requires methionine synthase and methylcobalamin; isolated methylmalonic acidemia without homocystinuria points away from this pathway.
Propionyl-CoA carboxylase converts propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA and requires biotin; deficiency causes propionic acidemia rather than an isolated block at methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and is unrelated to the characteristic methylmalonic acid accumulation.
Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency causes maple syrup urine disease and does not selectively block methylmalonyl-CoA conversion.
key_expl: Normal adenosylcobalamin synthesis with isolated methylmalonic acid accumulation points to the mutase itself. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase directly converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix.
objective: Identify the metabolic reaction catalyzed by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and distinguish isolated mutase deficiency from defects of propionyl-CoA carboxylase and cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Patent urachus from persistence of the allantoic connection between bladder dome and umbilicus
mechanism: The urachus derives from the intraembryonic allantoic connection between the developing bladder and umbilicus and normally obliterates. Complete persistence creates a patent tract that can drain urine from the umbilicus.
vignette: A term newborn has persistent clear fluid leaking from the umbilicus. The drainage increases during urination. Ultrasound shows a continuous tubular tract extending from the dome of the urinary bladder to the umbilicus.
lead: Which congenital anomaly is most likely?
distractors: Omphalomesenteric fistula
Urachal cyst
Umbilical-urachal sinus
Vesicourachal diverticulum
distractor_notes: An omphalomesenteric fistula connects ileum to the umbilicus and may drain enteric contents rather than urine from a tract continuous with the bladder.
A urachal cyst retains a closed central segment and does not create a complete bladder-to-umbilicus channel for urine drainage.
An umbilical-urachal sinus is open at the umbilical end but closed toward the bladder, so it does not produce urine leakage that increases with voiding.
A vesicourachal diverticulum remains open toward the bladder but closed at the umbilical end and therefore does not drain through the umbilicus.
key_expl: Urine leaking from the umbilicus and imaging of a continuous tract from the bladder dome to the umbilicus are diagnostic of a patent urachus, caused by persistence of the allantoic/urachal lumen.
objective: Differentiate a patent urachus from other urachal remnants and an omphalomesenteric fistula by recognizing urine drainage through a complete bladder-to-umbilicus tract.
clues: tract from bladder dome to umbilicus

diagnosis: Berkson bias is a hospital-selection bias caused when exposure and disease independently affect the probability of hospitalization
mechanism: In hospital-based case-control studies, selection into the study can depend jointly on the disease and the exposure or exposure-related conditions. If the exposure influences hospitalization among potential controls, the exposure prevalence in hospital controls can differ from that in the source population, biasing the estimated exposure-disease odds ratio.
vignette: Investigators conduct a case-control study of whether chronic alcohol use is associated with acute pancreatitis. Cases are patients admitted with pancreatitis. Controls are selected from other hospitalized patients. Chronic alcohol use also increases the probability of hospitalization for several conditions used to select controls, so alcohol use is more common among eligible hospital controls than in the community that generated the cases.
lead: Which specific bias is most directly introduced by this control-selection strategy?
distractors: Neyman prevalence-incidence bias
Recall bias
Interviewer bias
Immortal time bias
distractor_notes: Neyman bias results from using prevalent rather than incident cases when disease duration or survival is related to exposure; the stem instead describes differential hospital selection.
Recall bias requires systematic differences in retrospective exposure recall between cases and controls; the exposure distortion here arises before data collection through hospitalization.
Interviewer bias reflects systematic differences in how investigators elicit or record information; no differential interviewing is described.

Immortal time bias arises when a period during follow-up in which an outcome cannot occur is misclassified in an observational cohort; it does not explain biased exposure prevalence among hospital controls.
key_expl: This is Berkson bias, a specific hospital-selection bias. Because the exposure affects the probability that potential controls are hospitalized, hospital controls do not reproduce the exposure distribution of the source population, distorting the case-control odds ratio.
objective: Recognize Berkson bias in a hospital-based case-control study when exposure-related hospitalization alters the exposure distribution among selected controls.
clues: control exposure prevalence differs from source population
